titleText.es: Creo que el IETF alzancó un equilibrio perfecto con lo de los 128 bits. Podemos meter las direcciones MAC en una subred /64, y los nanobots solo podrán devorar medio planeta.
titleText.en: I think the IETF hit the right balance with the 128 bits thing. We can fit MAC addresses in a /64 subnet, and the nanobots will only be able to devour half the planet.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish title attribute is preserved exactly, including its printed typo alzancó. Spanish OCR corrections restore QUÉ twice, DIRECCIONES, DEBERÍAMOS, MICRAS, CÚBICAS, the punctuation around ¿POR?, and the opening exclamation mark before SE. The percentage, year, and IPv6 label are audited non-lexical exclusions.

regions.labelEs: COMANDANTE VENGA RÁPIDO SON LOS NANOBOTS SE HAN DETENIDO

applications.explanationEn: Venga is the formal one-person command of venir, asking the commander to come.
Son is a form of ser because los nanobots identifies what the reported objects are rather than where they are.
Se marks detenerse: the nanobots themselves came to a stop.
Han is the present helper for a plural subject, and detenido is the completed-action form.

regions.labelEs: HAN DEVORADO EL 40% DE LA TIERRA Y ENTONCES HAN PARADO SE HAN QUEDADO AHÍ QUIETOS

excludedUnits.rationale: 40% is a numeric percentage, not a Spanish lexical word occurrence.

applications.explanationEn: Han is the plural present helper and devorado is the completed-action form.
Han is the plural present helper and parado supplies the completed action.
Han is the plural present helper and quedado supplies the completed result.
Se and quedado form quedarse, and quietos names the resulting still state.
Por qué is written as two words with an accent when it asks for a reason.

regions.labelEs: ES UN MISTERIO A MENOS QUE QUÉ VOLUMEN TIENE CADA NANOBOT

applications.explanationEn: Es is a form of ser because un misterio classifies what the situation is rather than locating it.
A menos que opens a possible exception to the mystery.
Qué carries an accent because it asks which volume or amount.
Cúbicas follows micras as its neutral technical description.
Cúbicas uses feminine plural -as to match micras.
The speaker repeats the reason question with qué left understood.

regions.labelEs: CREO QUE EL AÑO 1998 NOS HA HECHO GANAR ALGO DE TIEMPO

excludedUnits.rationale: 1998 is a printed year, not a Spanish lexical word occurrence.

applications.explanationEn: Ha is the singular present helper and hecho is hacer’s completed-action form.
Nos marks the affected group, ha hecho supplies the matching form of hacer, and ganar is the unchanged action verb.
Ganar and tiempo form the conventional expression for obtaining extra time.

regions.labelEs: QUÉ QUIERES DECIR CON DIRECCIONES AGOTADAS

applications.explanationEn: Qué keeps its accent because it asks what meaning is intended.
Quieres changes for the listener, while decir stays in its dictionary form; together they ask about meaning.
Agotadas follows direcciones as its neutral description.
Agotadas uses feminine plural -as to match direcciones.

regions.labelEs: MIRA DEBERÍAMOS HABER MIGRADO DE IPv6 HACE EONES

excludedUnits.rationale: IPv6 is a protocol name containing letters and a digit, not a Spanish lexical word occurrence.

applications.explanationEn: Mira is the affirmative command for one familiar listener and works here as an attention getter.
Deberíamos changes for “we” and haber stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Haber is unchanged and migrado supplies the completed action.
Hace comes before the length of time to say how long ago.

cards.noteEn: A comandante is the person in charge of a military unit or operation.

cards.answerEn: Use the usted command form: regular -ar verbs end in -e, while regular -er and -ir verbs end in -a.
cards.noteEn: Usted is the polite or formal singular “you.” Hablar becomes hable, comer becomes coma, and escribir becomes escriba. Usted is usually left out because the command ending already shows formal address. Some common verbs are irregular, such as decir → diga.
cards.questionEn: How do you politely tell one person to do something in Spanish?

cards.promptEs: ser para identidad · estar para ubicación
cards.questionEn: Which Spanish “to be” verb says what something is, and which says where it is?
cards.answerEn: Use ser for identity or a defining description; use estar for the location of a person or thing.
cards.noteEn: This contrast is not simply permanent versus temporary. Forms of ser such as soy and es identify or describe what something is. Forms of estar such as están normally locate people and things. Events are a common exception: Spanish uses ser to say where or when an event takes place.

example.es: El museo es famoso y está en Madrid.
example.en: The museum is famous and is in Madrid.

cards.answerEn: IPv6’s original specification appeared in 1998; the joke treats an IPv6 address block as the finite supply of identities available to a nanobot swarm.
cards.noteEn: The core IPv6 specification, RFC 2460, was published in 1998. IPv4’s limited address space motivated IPv6, whose 128-bit addresses are unimaginably numerous. The comic imagines self-replicating nanobots stopping after consuming only part of Earth because their swarm was still assigned too small an IPv6 subnet and ran out of addresses.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks detenerse, “to stop”
cards.noteEn: With a form of detener, se shows that the people or things themselves come to a stop.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

cards.noteEn: After a form of haber, detenido is detenerse’s completed-action form here.
This sense names the planet rather than land or soil.

example.es: La Tierra gira alrededor del Sol.

cards.noteEn: After a form of haber, parado presents the stopping as completed.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks quedarse, “to remain” or “stay”
cards.noteEn: Quedar and quedarse have several uses. With se here, the subject continues to be present rather than leaving.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone remains in, or ends up in, a particular state?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of quedarse followed by a word that names the resulting or continuing state.
cards.noteEn: The plus sign in the prompt means that the state word follows quedarse. Quedarse is pronominal: it comes with me, te, se, nos, or os even though no one literally remains themselves. Change quedar and its small marker to match the person and time. When another verb has already changed for the person, the marker may stand before that verb: se puede quedar.

example.es: Después de la noticia, Pablo se quedó callado.
example.en: After the news, Pablo fell silent.

cards.answerEn: ended up; remained (completed form of quedarse)
cards.noteEn: Quedado is used with a form of haber to place quedarse in a completed time. A following word can name the resulting state or place.
Ahí points to a place away from the speaker but normally not as distant as allí. The distinction varies by region and context.
Quietos is masculine plural because it describes more than one nanobot.
Write the question form as two words, with an accent on qué. Write the usual answer word porque as one word without an accent.
cards.questionEn: How do you write “why” and “because” in Spanish?

example.es: ¿Por qué estudias español? Porque me gusta.
example.en: Why do you study Spanish? Because I like it.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; begins a menos que, “unless”
cards.noteEn: A is fixed as the first part of the connector a menos que.

example.en: I will go unless it rains.

cards.questionEn: How do you introduce a possible exception that would change what you just said?
cards.noteEn: A menos que introduces a possible exception. The verb after it normally uses a special form because the exception is not presented as a fact; for example, llueve changes to llueva.

example.en: We will go unless it rains.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; middle of a menos que, “unless”
cards.noteEn: Menos is fixed between a and que in this connector.

example.en: We are leaving unless it snows.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes a menos que, “unless”
cards.noteEn: Que completes the connector and introduces the possible exception.

example.es: Ven, a menos que estés ocupado.

cards.noteEn: Qué goes directly before a noun when asking which member or type is meant. It keeps the written accent in a direct question and in an embedded question inside a larger statement.

example.en: I do not know which route to choose.

cards.answerEn: Write qué, cómo, cuándo, and similar words with an accent when they ask a question or add an exclamation.
cards.noteEn: This includes direct questions (¿Qué quieres?), questions inside another sentence (No sé qué quiere), and exclamations (¡Qué bonito!). Without the accent, these words usually connect parts of a sentence instead: el libro que quiero means “the book that I want.”
cards.questionEn: Why do words such as que, como, and cuando sometimes have a written accent?

cards.noteEn: Here volumen means how much physical space an object occupies, not sound level.

example.es: Calculamos el volumen de la caja.
example.en: We calculated the volume of the box.

cards.noteEn: A micra is the everyday Spanish name for a micrometre, one millionth of a metre.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.noteEn: Cúbicas is feminine plural to match micras.

example.es: La muestra ocupa cinco micras cúbicas.
example.en: The sample occupies five cubic micrometres.

cards.answerEn: why?; for what reason? (with qué left understood)
cards.noteEn: In the short echo ¿por?, the usual qué is omitted because the question being repeated is already clear.
Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.promptEs: hacer + persona + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone or something makes a person do an action?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of hacer, then the affected person, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The unchanged dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Only hacer changes for the person and time. A short word such as me, te, or nos usually marks who is made to act; in a compound form such as ha hecho, that short word comes before the helper ha.
Here hecho is the completed-action form of hacer in the pattern that makes someone do something.

example.es: La broma nos ha hecho reír.
example.en: The joke has made us laugh.

cards.noteEn: With tiempo, ganar means to obtain extra time before something happens.

example.es: La pausa nos permite ganar tiempo.
example.en: The pause lets us buy time.

cards.questionEn: How do you say “to gain time” or “to buy time”?
cards.answerEn: to gain time; to buy time
cards.noteEn: Ganar literally means to win or gain. With tiempo it conventionally means creating or obtaining extra time before a deadline or event.

example.es: Haz una pregunta para ganar tiempo.
example.en: Ask a question to buy time.

cards.noteEn: An enjambre is a large moving group, especially of insects or, by extension, tiny robots.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that a word, sign, or person means something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of querer followed by decir; together, querer decir means “to mean.”
cards.noteEn: Querer normally means “to want,” and decir means “to say.” As a unit, querer decir asks for or states the intended meaning. Only querer changes for the person and time; decir remains in its unchanged dictionary form.

cards.answerEn: by; when you say (introducing the wording being explained)
cards.noteEn: After querer decir, con can introduce the exact word or expression whose meaning is being asked about.
Direcciones can mean addresses or directions. With names and phone numbers, it refers to contact or location addresses.

example.es: Guardaron las direcciones de los clientes.

cards.noteEn: Here agotadas describes a supply of addresses that has all been used, not tired people.

cards.answerEn: look; listen; hey (to get someone's attention)
cards.noteEn: Mira is the positive command form of mirar used with one familiar person. At the start of a comment, it often simply gets the listener's attention, like “look,” “listen,” or “hey,” without asking them to look at an object.

cards.promptEs: orden afirmativa para tú: habla, come, escribe
cards.questionEn: How do you give one friend or familiar person a positive command?
cards.answerEn: Use the informal singular command form, often the same form used for “he” or “she” in the present.
cards.noteEn: For many regular verbs, -ar becomes -a and -er or -ir becomes -e: hablar becomes habla, comer becomes come, and escribir becomes escribe. Some common verbs are irregular or change their stem. Negative commands use a different form and are a separate pattern.
Deberíamos is the “we” form of deber used for advice or what ought to happen. The -ríamos ending adds the “would/should” viewpoint: deber becomes deberíamos.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone should or must do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of deber, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The unchanged dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Only deber changes for the person and time. Depending on context, deber can sound like advice, duty, or a strong requirement.

After a verb such as debería, haber remains in its dictionary form and combines with a completed-action form such as llamado or comido. In this construction, haber is a helper rather than the hay construction meaning “there is.”

cards.questionEn: How do you refer to an action that was already completed after another verb such as poder, deber, or parecer?
cards.answerEn: Use the unchanged helper haber followed by the completed-action form of the main verb.
cards.noteEn: The completed-action form is often called a participle: terminar becomes terminado, hacer becomes hecho, and ser becomes sido. After another verb, haber stays unchanged. The plus sign in the prompt means “followed by.”
After haber, migrado is migrar’s completed-action form.

example.es: La empresa ha migrado al sistema nuevo.
example.en: The company has migrated to the new system.

cards.noteEn: Before a length of time, hace tells you how long ago something happened. It does not mean “does” in this use.

cards.questionEn: How do you say how long ago a past event happened?
cards.answerEn: Put hace before the length of time.
cards.noteEn: Spanish places hace before a duration: hace dos semanas means “two weeks ago.” The verb that describes the event itself is normally in a past form.
